claim: Two monkeys (Macaca mulatta) completed 29,726 trials (Monkey A: 10,748; Monkey H: 18,978).
source: Two monkeys (Macaca mulatta) completed 29,726 trials (Monkey A: 10,748; Monkey H: 18,978).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of trials completed by each monkey subject.

claim: Subjects performed the task with high accuracy despite its challenging nature.
source: Despite the challenging nature of the task, subjects were able to perform it with high accuracy (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A-B showing psychometric functions indicating high accuracy.

claim: Subjects demonstrated a primacy bias such that early stimuli have stronger temporal weights than later stimuli.
source: We found that the subjects utilised all eight stimuli throughout the trial to inform their decision, and demonstrated a primacy bias such that early stimuli have stronger temporal weights than later stimuli (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing temporal weights (Figure 2C-D) and is consistent with bounded evidence integration.

claim: A primacy bias has been reported in prior studies in monkeys and is consistent with a decision-making strategy of bounded evidence integration.
source: A primacy bias has been reported in prior studies in monkeys, and is consistent with a decision-making strategy of bounded evidence integration (Kiani et al., 2008; Nienborg and Cumming, 2009; Wimmer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim cites previous literature (Kiani et al., 2008; Nienborg and Cumming, 2009; Wimmer et al., 2015) to support the observation.

claim: Monkeys were more accurate on 'Broad Correct' trials than on 'Narrow Correct' trials.
source: The monkeys are more accurate on 'Broad Correct' trials than on 'Narrow Correct' trials (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Statistical test (Chi-squared test, chi = 99.05, p<1×10−10) and Figure 3B support this claim.

claim: In 'Ambiguous' trials, monkeys demonstrated a preference for the broadly distributed stream.
source: Furthermore, in the 'Ambiguous' trials, the monkeys demonstrated a preference for the broadly distributed stream, which has greater variability across samples (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Binomial test (p<1×10−10) and Figure 3C demonstrate the preference for the broad option.

claim: The pro-variance bias pattern of decision behaviour in monkeys is similar to what was found in human subjects.
source: Such a pro-variance bias pattern of decision behaviour is similar to what was found in human subjects (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Tsetsos et al., 2012; Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim references previous human studies (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Tsetsos et al., 2012) and compares to Figure 3D-E.

claim: Evidence variability was a significant predictor of choice in monkeys.
source: Regression analysis confirmed that evidence variability was a significant predictor of choice (Figure 4D; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Regression analysis (t = 19.65, p<10−10) shown in Figure 4D supports this claim.

claim: The PVB index across both monkeys was 0.173 (Monkey A = 0.230; Monkey H = 0.138) from 'Regular' trials.
source: From the 'Regular' trials, the PVB index across both monkeys was 0.173 (Monkey A = 0.230; Monkey H = 0.138).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the calculated PVB index values.

claim: Cross-validation revealed choice was principally driven by the mean evidence, verifying that subjects performed the task using evidence accumulation.
source: A cross-validation approach revealed choice was principally driven by the mean evidence, verifying that subjects performed the task using evidence accumulation (Supplementary file 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Cross-validation analysis (Supplementary file 1) supports that mean evidence is the primary driver of choice.

claim: Cross-validation revealed that choices were better described by a model incorporating evidence variability, rather than the extreme sample values.
source: Cross-validation revealed that choices were better described by a model incorporating evidence variability, rather than the extreme sample values (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Cross-validation analysis (Supplementary file 2) comparing models supports this claim.

claim: Neither monkey subject demonstrated a 'frequent winner' bias after controlling for the influence of mean evidence on choices.
source: After controlling for the influence of mean evidence on choices, we found that neither subject demonstrated a 'frequent winner' bias.
evidence: Regression analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) shows no significant frequent winner bias.

claim: The spiking circuit model demonstrated a pro-variance bias comparable to the monkeys.
source: Importantly, not only can the circuit model perform the evidence accumulation task, it also demonstrated a pro-variance bias comparable to the monkeys (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: Figure 5C-F shows the circuit model's performance on narrow-broad and regular trials demonstrating pro-variance bias.

claim: The circuit model demonstrated a temporal profile which decays over time, similar to the monkeys.
source: The temporal process of evidence integration in the circuit model disproportionately weighted early stimuli over late stimuli (Figure 5G), similar to the evidence integration patterns observed in both monkeys.
evidence: Figure 5G shows temporal regression weights for the circuit model matching the primacy bias observed in monkeys.

claim: The mean-field model demonstrated similar decision-making behaviour to the spiking circuit.
source: To understand the origin of the pro-variance bias in the spiking circuit, we mathematically reduced the circuit model to a mean-field model (Figure 6A), which demonstrated similar decision-making behaviour to the spiking circuit (Figure 6B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 6B-C shows psychometric functions and regression analysis for the mean-field model.

claim: A momentarily strong stimulus has an asymmetrically greater influence upon the decision-making process than a momentarily weak stimulus, leading to pro-variance bias.
source: This example provides an intuitive explanation for the pro-variance bias: a momentarily strong stimulus has an asymmetrically greater influence upon the decision-making process than a momentarily weak stimulus.
evidence: Phase-plane analysis (Figure 6E-H) demonstrates this asymmetry arising from expansive non-linearities.

claim: Such asymmetry arises from the expansive non-linearities of the firing rate profiles.
source: Such asymmetry arises from the expansive non-linearities of the firing rate profiles (Figure 6D, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Figure 6D shows the firing rate profile with expansive non-linearity (positive second derivative).

claim: The circuit model demonstrated a smaller PVB index for trials with more total evidence than for trials with less total evidence.
source: The circuit model demonstrated a smaller PVB index (larger mean evidence and smaller evidence standard deviation regression weights) for trials with more total evidence than for trials with less total evidence (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2C shows PVB index comparison between high and low total evidence trials.

claim: The lowered E/I circuit increases the PVB index relative to the control model.
source: The lowered E/I circuit increases the PVB index relative to the control model (permutation test, p=6×10−5), while the elevated E/I circuit decreases the PVB index (permutation test, p<10−5).
evidence: Statistical tests and Figure 7H demonstrate dissociable predictions for E/I perturbations on PVB index.

claim: The PVB index is roughly maintained in the sensory deficit circuit.
source: The PVB index is roughly maintained in the sensory deficit circuit (permutation test, p=0.6933).
evidence: Statistical test (p=0.6933) and Figure 7H show no significant change in PVB index for sensory deficit.

claim: Ketamine yielded an increase in subjects' PVB, consistent with lowered cortical excitation/inhibition balance from NMDA-R hypofunction predominantly onto excitatory neurons.
source: Ketamine yielded an increase in subjects' PVB, consistent with lowered cortical excitation/inhibition balance from NMDA-R hypofunction predominantly onto excitatory neurons.
evidence: Experimental data (Figure 8F) shows increased PVB index under ketamine, matching the lowered E/I model prediction.

claim: Following ketamine administration, subjects' choice accuracy was markedly decreased.
source: Following ketamine administration, subjects' choice accuracy was markedly decreased (Figure 8A), without a significant shift in their strategies (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Figure 8A shows time course of accuracy decrease after ketamine injection.

claim: Ketamine significantly reduces the regression coefficient for mean evidence.
source: Ketamine significantly reduces the coefficient (permutation test, p<1×10−6), reflecting a drop in choice accuracy.
evidence: Statistical test (p<1×10−6) and Figure 8D demonstrate reduced mean evidence coefficient under ketamine.

claim: Ketamine does not significantly reduce the evidence standard deviation regression coefficient.
source: Ketamine does not significantly reduce the coefficient (permutation test, p=0.152).
evidence: Statistical test (p=0.152) and Figure 8E show no significant reduction in evidence SD coefficient.

claim: Ketamine increases the PVB index.
source: Ketamine increases the PVB index (permutation test, p=8×10−6), consistent with the model prediction of the lowered E/I circuit.
evidence: Statistical test (p=8×10−6) and Figure 8F demonstrate increased PVB index under ketamine.

claim: Ketamine significantly increased the subjects' lapse rate.
source: Consistent with the psychometric function (Figure 8C), we found that ketamine significantly increased the subjects' lapse rate (Subject A: Lapse(Saline)=1.49×10−11, Lapse(Ketamine)=0.118, permutation test, p<0.0001; Subject H: Lapse(Saline)=0.012, Lapse(Ketamine)=0.0684, permutation test, p=0.019).
evidence: Statistical tests show significant increase in lapse rate for both subjects under ketamine.

claim: The PVB effect was still present in the regression model that included the effect of lapses.
source: Crucially, however, the PVB effect was still present in the regression model that included the effect of lapses.
evidence: Analysis controlling for lapse rate (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) confirms PVB effect persists.

claim: The change in lapse rate was not responsible for any of the behavioural effects of ketamine.
source: This confirms that the change in lapse rate was not responsible for any of the behavioural effects of ketamine outlined above.
evidence: Analysis controlling for lapse rate shows PVB effect is independent of lapse rate changes.

claim: Quantitative model comparison revealed the effect of ketamine injection on monkey choice behaviour was better explained by lowered E/I perturbations in the circuit model, than by sensory deficit or elevated E/I perturbations.
source: Quantitative model comparison, using cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, revealed the effect of ketamine injection on monkey choice behaviour was better explained by lowered E/I perturbations in the circuit model, than by sensory deficit or elevated E/I perturbations (Figure 8—figure supplements 4–6).
evidence: Multiple quantitative measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, KL divergence) shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 4-6 support this claim.

claim: Ketamine caused a general downward shift of the temporal weights but had no strong effects on how each stimulus was weighted relative to the others in the stream.
source: It caused a general downward shift of the temporal weights; but had no strong effects on how each stimulus was weighted relative to the others in the stream.
evidence: Figure 8G shows temporal weighting patterns under ketamine vs saline.

claim: The behavioural effects of ketamine are most consistent with lowered E/I balance and weakened recurrent connections.
source: This shifting of the weights could reflect a sensory deficit, but given the results of the pro-variance analysis, collectively the behavioural effects of ketamine are most consistent with lowered E/I balance and weakened recurrent connections.
evidence: Integration of multiple analyses (PVB index, temporal weights, model comparison) supports this conclusion.

claim: NMDA-R hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.
source: For example, one line of research has implicated N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-R) hypofunction in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia (Nakazawa et al., 2012; Kehrer et al., 2008; Olney and Farber, 1995).
evidence: The claim cites multiple references (Nakazawa et al., 2012; Kehrer et al., 2008; Olney and Farber, 1995) supporting this hypothesis.

claim: Subanaesthetic doses (~0.1–0.5 mg/kg) of the NMDA-R antagonist ketamine produce psychotomimetic effects in humans, especially cognitive aspects.
source: Some of the strongest evidence in support of this hypothesis comes from the observation that subanaesthetic doses (~0.1–0.5 mg/kg) of the NMDA-R antagonist ketamine produce psychotomimetic effects in humans, especially cognitive aspects (Krystal et al., 1994; Umbricht et al., 2000; Malhotra et al., 1996; see Frohlich and Van Horn, 2014 for review).
evidence: Multiple citations (Krystal et al., 1994; Umbricht et al., 2000; Malhotra et al., 1996; Frohlich and Van Horn, 2014) support this observation.

claim: NMDA-Rs have long been argued to play a central role in temporally extended cognitive processes such as working memory.
source: For example, NMDA-Rs have long been argued to play a central role in temporally extended cognitive processes such as working memory, supported by studies of the effects of NMDA-R antagonism in prefrontal cortical microcircuits (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation (Wang et al., 2013) supports the role of NMDA-Rs in working memory.

claim: Using a cortical circuit model, a precise pattern of working memory deficits can be predicted by hypofunction of NMDA-Rs, eliciting changes in excitation-inhibition balance.
source: Using a cortical circuit model, a precise pattern of working memory deficits can be predicted by hypofunction of NMDA-Rs, eliciting changes in excitation-inhibition balance (E/I ratio) (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation (Murray et al., 2014) describes circuit model predictions for working memory deficits.

claim: Circuit model predictions are consistent with those observed in healthy volunteers administered with ketamine and in patients with schizophrenia.
source: This predicts changes in behaviour consistent with those observed in healthy volunteers administered with ketamine (Murray et al., 2014), and also in patients with schizophrenia (Starc et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations (Murray et al., 2014; Starc et al., 2017) support consistency between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: When choosing between two series of bars with distinct heights, people have a preference to choose the option where evidence is more broadly distributed across samples.
source: For instance, when choosing between two series of bars with distinct heights, people have a preference to choose the option where evidence is more broadly distributed across samples (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Tsetsos et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations (Tsetsos et al., 2016; Tsetsos et al., 2012) document the pro-variance bias in humans.

claim: The pro-variance bias becomes the optimal strategy when the accumulation process is contaminated by noise.
source: Although this 'pro-variance bias' may appear irrational, and would not be captured by many normative decision-making models, it becomes the optimal strategy when the accumulation process is contaminated by noise (Tsetsos et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation (Tsetsos et al., 2016) provides theoretical justification for pro-variance bias under noisy accumulation.

claim: Biophysically grounded computational modelling of cortical circuits has been an influential technique used to investigate evidence accumulation at the mechanistic level.
source: As with working memory, an influential technique used to investigate evidence accumulation at the mechanistic level has been biophysically grounded computational modelling of cortical circuits (Wang, 2002; Wong and Wang, 2006; Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations (Wang, 2002; Wong and Wang, 2006; Murray et al., 2017) document the use of circuit models for evidence accumulation.

claim: Neural circuit models bridge synaptic and behavioural levels of understanding by predicting both choices and their underlying neural activity.
source: Crucially, these neural circuit models bridge synaptic and behavioural levels of understanding, by predicting both choices and their underlying neural activity.
evidence: This describes a key property of neural circuit models in linking different levels of analysis.

claim: Circuit model predictions reproduce key experimental phenomena, mirroring the behavioural and neurophysiological data recorded from macaque monkeys performing evidence accumulation tasks.
source: These predictions reproduce key experimental phenomena, mirroring the behavioural and neurophysiological data recorded from macaque monkeys performing evidence accumulation tasks (Wang, 2002; Wong et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations (Wang, 2002; Wong et al., 2007) support the correspondence between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The dose of ketamine used was 0.5 mg/kg, intramuscular injection.
source: These model predictions were tested experimentally by administering monkeys with a subanaesthetic dose of the NMDA-R antagonist ketamine (0.5 mg/kg, intramuscular injection).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ketamine dose and route of administration.

claim: The control circuit model completed 94,000 'Regular' trials.
source: The control circuit model completed 94,000 'Regular' trials, where both streams were narrow in 25% of the trials, both streams were broad in 25% of the trials, and one stream was narrow and one was broad in 50% of the trials (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of trials simulated in the control model.

claim: The control model also completed 47,000 standard session Narrow-Broad trials.
source: The control model also completed 47,000 standard session Narrow-Broad trials.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of narrow-broad trials simulated.

claim: The mean-field model completed 94,000 standard session 'Regular' trials.
source: The mean-field model completed 94,000 standard session 'Regular' trials, in the same manner as the circuit models.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of trials simulated in the mean-field model.

claim: Monkey A completed 41 standard sessions and 28 pharmacological sessions (15 ketamine; 13 saline).
source: Monkey A completed 41 standard sessions, and 28 pharmacological sessions (15 ketamine; 13 saline).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of sessions for Monkey A.

claim: Monkey H completed 68 standard sessions and 35 pharmacological sessions (18 ketamine; 17 saline).
source: Monkey H completed 68 standard sessions, and 35 pharmacological sessions (18 ketamine; 17 saline).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of sessions for Monkey H.

claim: The data collected during the ketamine effect period formed a behavioural database of 8521 completed trials.
source: The data collected during this period formed a behavioural database of 8521 completed trials (Monkey A Saline: 1710; Monkey A Ketamine: 2276; Monkey H Saline: 2669; Monkey H Ketamine: 1866).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of trials in the pharmacological experiment database.

claim: The subjects weighed 12–13.3 kg and were ~6 years old at the start of the data collection period.
source: The subjects weighed 12–13.3 kg, and both were ~6 years old at the start of the data collection period.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the physical characteristics of the subjects.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the UCL Local Ethical Procedures Committee and the UK Home Office (PPL Number 70/8842).
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the UCL Local Ethical Procedures Committee and the UK Home Office (PPL Number 70/8842), and carried out in accordance with the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states ethical approval information.
